what_it_does: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are cryptographic techniques that let one party convince another that a computation was done correctly without revealing the underlying data — used in privacy-preserving blockchains and verifiable AI. A specific ZKP scheme called zkSTARK relies heavily on a hashing algorithm named Poseidon and on a data structure called a Merkle tree (imagine a tree where each node contains a fingerprint — a hash — of all the data beneath it, so that tampering anywhere in the tree is immediately detectable). The bottleneck is that computing thousands or millions of Poseidon hashes to build these trees is very slow on general-purpose processors. This paper presents AcclMT, a hardware accelerator built on an FPGA (a chip that can be programmed to behave like custom hardware) that speeds up Poseidon-hash-based Merkle tree construction. The design improves efficiency by reusing modular arithmetic units (the most expensive building blocks) more thoroughly, caching intermediate hash values in on-chip memory to reduce data movement, and scheduling tasks carefully to keep the hardware busy.
